content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors introduce a novel architecture named MILE that can learn to solve math word problems by exploiting an external memory module, which is manipulated through attention mechanisms. They also argue that tree-structured formula representations do not allow to effectively process all kind of mathematical problems, and thus propose an alternative formula representation based on a segmented sequence. Performance gains of MILE are demonstrated by comparing it against other state-of-the-art methods using the Math23K dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
A strength of the proposed architecture is that it combines several ideas and processing mechanisms into a unified framework, and apparently this leads to some performance gains. Another strength is the use of a popular benchmarking dataset (Math23k), which allows to compare model performance against other existing methods.

The major weakness, in my opinion, is that the model architecture is quite convoluted, and the graphical/textual description provided by the authors does not allow to easily understand its detailed functioning. Furthermore, results presented in Table 2 suggest that the MILE architecture might not be particularly effective in several cases (as also recognized by the authors). In fact, it achieves worse accuracy in the LSTM/Tree and Graph/Tree comparison, and only modestly improve in the BERT/Tree condition. Such minor improvement might not justify such an increase in model complexity. Additional analyses would help in clarifying the role of different modules (e.g., the memory) in achieving the final performance, since up to this point the major advantage seems to be provided by the use of large-scale language models (BERT) during the decoding phase. Another weak point is that the authors in the Introduction explicitly refer to a class of math problems that cannot be properly represented by tree-like structures, in order to motivate their alternative formula representation. I would thus expect the authors to systematically probe their method also in these specific cases, in order to highlight the effective benefit of their alternative formulation.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: Although the paper is readable, English phrasing and grammar should be improved. Also the model description should be significantly improved; for example:
- The model architecture is fairly sophisticated, which makes it challenging to describe in a few pages. However, I think that Fig. 1 can be refined, for example by making sure that all variables / entities described in the text (4.2 and 4.3) are also reported in the figure.
- There is not always a good match between the steps described in the text (e.g., Initialization equations) and the corresponding representation in the figure (e.g., it seems that the Initialization equations also involve the encoding phase in Fig. 1).
- In the text described at page 4 (and Fig. 1) it is not clear how the encoder embedding and the encoder summary are related.
- Some variables in the equations are not explicitly defined (e.g., Wc in eq. 7). One might intuitively guess what they stand for, but it would be useful to make sure everything is explicitly and clearly defined.
- How is k tuned during the Operand Decoding phase?
- I was not able to fully understand the ready/write memory mechanism (Memory Update): is it working like a memory stack, or does the memory have an addressing mechanism? It would be useful to describe it more in detail.

Quality: The experimental setup seems appropriate. One daunting question that might arise, however, is related to the generalization capabilities of the model: given the quick deterioration of performance in the number-p and formula-p conditions, I wonder whether this architecture could really generalize to conditions that were never seen during training.

Novelty: The proposed architecture seems original and well-motivated. Related work is properly referenced and discussed.

Reproducibility: The authors declared that the complete source code will be published following publication, so I think the results are in principle reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I found this paper interesting and stimulating. At the same time, however, the writing should be significantly improved, and in general it is not clear whether the performance gains reported justify the increase in complexity of the model architecture. Further analyses are also required to better understand the computational role of different modules of the architecture and to establish whether the model can really generalize to novel problems.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer BhQA
content.comment:
Clarity:

We are deeply sorry for any points that we didn't make clear enough and brought trouble to your reading. Here are some direct explanations to your concerns, and we have refashioned the figure and improved the writing in the revision.

· The encoder embedding and the encoder summary are not directly and necessarily related. They are just the two common outputs of any typical sentence encoder. To be more exact, encoder embedding is the embedding of each token of the input sequence, and encoder summary is the summary of the whole input sequence.

· $W_c$ is the width of constant embedding (or say the length of $T_{con}$) as mentioned at the end of page 4.

· k is the index of the operand to be decoded. So it traverses from 1 to the count of necessary operands for an operator (e.g., 2 for + and 1 for log())

· The read/write mechanism works with addressing. Because there is a bijection between the valid memory addresses and possible operands (Section 4.1), the address to read from or write to is determined once $opd_{i,k}$ is decoded.

Generalization capability:

We absolutely agree with you that the difficulty of generalizing to truly harder conditions (roughly measured by the counter of numbers or length of formulas) is extremely high, and it's the very reason that makes the quick accuracy deterioration. But this is also a common challenge faced by all existing methods, and our proposed method has done better than other baselines (shown by the accuracy and curves). We consider the further improvement in generalizing to these harder conditions as an open question for future work.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors propose MILE, which employs a memory buffer to perform a non-tree structure mathematical calculation. 
The contributions that the authors claim are:
1. A new representation for non-tree-based formula
2. A new decoding method that supports the representation 
3. Accuracy, robustness, and generalizability are improved compared to the existing methods
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The representation is new but the intuition of constructing this representation is clear.

Weakness: 
1. The clarity is an issue,  especially on the mathematical formula part. There are just so many subscripts going along with the neural network architecture, for example, $ N_{mupd|opr_{i},k}$. Figure 1 is very complex and full of details. However, too many details in one graph are quite confusing. Indeed, I still cannot fully comprehend figure 1 even though I believe I understand mathematics. 
2. The fairness of the experiments. The authors utilize a data augmentation technique called formula mutation(FM) in their approach. They claim that MILE is the only model that benefits from the formula mutation, but only comparing to one baseline. Observing the major outcome and the FM, I wonder whether the performance gain is due to the hard-coded knowledge that  $+$ and $\cdot$ are commutative. Because the baseline which uses graph representation can kind of capture the commutativity, it performs better than MILE. To alleviate this concern, a study with/without FM should be performed with regard to different baselines.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: 1.5/5
Pros: The intuition to include the non-tree-based formulas is pretty clear. 
Cons:
1. Mathematical formula is hard to comprehend with the subscripts.
2. Figure 1 illustrating the pipeline is confusing.

Quality: 2.5/5
Pros: The representation of the non-tree-based formula is theoretically justifiable.
Cons:
1. The experiment design could be an unfair comparison.
2. The generalizability experiment design is somewhat confusing without the number-0.0, and formula-0.0 to understand the baseline performance for pure generalizability ability. 
3. It would be nice if a model size comparison is included in the experiment part.

Originality: 3.5/5
The authors introduce a novel representation of non-tree-based formulas and introduce a decoder designed for the representation. However, the advantage of this design compared to the baselines is not well justified.

However, there are a few flaws in both clarity and experiment design. These issues undermine the credibility that this work outperforms the baselines in accuracy, robustness, and generalizability.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer phMo
content.comment:
Clarity:

We are deeply sorry for any points that we didn't make clear enough and brought trouble to your reading. We have simplified the subscripts in the equations and refashioned the figure to improve its intelligibility. We hope they are easier to be followed now.

Experiment:

Actually, we did conduct the comparison on all nine model implementations. The same phenomenon is observed on all three encoders, so we only report the comparison on BERT encoder because it is most representative. We have included all the results in the revision of our paper. (The only exception happens on LSTM encoder + LSTM decoder. We explain this result by saying that the LSTM encoder and decoder are too weak and be likely to overfit. But the formula mutation can prevent overfitting.)

Generalizability experiment:

We are sorry that we may not make the explanation clear enough. Actually, all number-p and formula-p are testing the pure generalizability ability because there is always no overlap between the training and test samples. There is no pre-split training and test sets in the Math23K dataset (except for the public test set), so in each of these experiments, we split the whole dataset manually into the training set with (1-p) of samples and the test set with p of the rest samples. As a result, number-0.0 and formula-0.0 make no sense.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces an architecture to solve problems from the Math23K dataset, which contains math word problems. The architecture is inspired by the neural Turing machine. It starts with an arbitrary encoder for the text question and focuses on the decoder, which is structured along the formula that computes the result of the question.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
My main concern is that the Math23K dataset is very simple, this architecture is very specialized to the type of problems in this dataset, and the results improve only marginal over an old transformer-style architecture (BERT). There are other datasets around, such as GSM8k that have additional comparison points.

There has been a lot of related work on formula representations and math word problems over the last couple of years and the general insight seems to be that large language models (e.g. PaLM) are very strong on these tasks nowadays. This is not compared to or discussed in this paper.

Another line of work to consider would be chain-of-thought prompting, which has significantly improved the reasoning abilities of transformer models.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity and quality of the write-up are good.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper suggests an architecture specialized to simple math word problems, but achieves only marginal benefits over BERT. Newer transformer-based architectures and approaches are not considered.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer qCSe
content.comment:
Dataset selection:

We didn't report the result on GSM8k because of its limited amount of effective training samples. Actually, we did survey the applicability of the GSM8k dataset. There are 7473 training samples in its training set, which is already relatively quite few for a mathematical reasoning and NLP task. What's worse, after data preprocessing, we found that only 5745 of these samples are valid for training a formula-based method. This is not because the answers or solutions are incorrect, but because the calculation flows in the annotations are not always continuous. This means that sometimes there come values in the solutions that are neither numbers in the question, nor common constants, nor intermediate results in previous steps. The influence of this trouble may be limited on other baseline methods (e.g., chain-of-thought) based on natural language prediction, but it will completely destroy the establishment of formulas and make the corresponding samples unusable in formula-based methods. As a result, we considered GSM8k not quite suitable for the experiment in this work. There are indeed some other available datasets such as MathQA, but many of them also have their own problems like noise. As a result, as we stated in the paper, Math23K is the most suitable dataset that meets all the requests on this task to the best of our knowledge.

Related work:

We considered these works as prompting methods in the original manuscript of our paper and mentioned them in the last paragraph of Section 2.2. We have rearranged Section 2.2 and added more discussions on these methods in the revision. Thank you for your comments.

Contribution:

To achieve higher accuracy is not the only motivation of our work. Our other contributions include supporting non-tree-structured formulas and improving the generalization capacity and robustness.
